Storage Administration

1. Storage Administration

A cloud disk has been enlarged, but the application still reports no space. The provider changed the outer block device; the partition, logical volume, or filesystem inside it may still have the old size. Storage administration is the work of identifying these layers and changing them in the correct order.

This chapter begins with inspection and uses a file-backed filesystem for its worked lab. Real-device formatting is destructive. A device name in a book is never sufficient evidence that a disk is safe to erase.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — Chapter 9 — Storage Administration

2. Check capacity at the correct layer

A filesystem can run out of inodes before bytes. Check the exact mount serving the failing path. Free space on one filesystem does not help a different full mount.

SOURCE: Check capacity at the correct layer

3. Chapter 9 — Storage Administration

A cloud disk has been enlarged, but the application still reports no space. The provider changed the outer block device; the partition, logical volume, or filesystem inside it may still have the old size. SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — Chapter 9 — Storage Administration

4. 9.1 Linux Storage Architecture

A typical path from application data to hardware can include a file, filesystem, logical volume, partition, block device, storage controller, and physical media. Not every system uses every layer. A filesystem can live directly on a block device, and cloud or virtual storage adds layers outside the guest.

Each layer has its own identity, size, and failure modes. A larger disk does not automatically enlarge its filesystem. A healthy filesystem does not prove the physical storage is reliable.

Draw the actual stack before changing it. Use findmnt, lsblk, and, where applicable, LVM tools. Record which layer owns the change requested by the application team. The correct command follows from that model, not from the phrase “add space.”

Linux example — 9.1

Observe disks, partitions, and mounts together.

What to check: This establishes relationships before any device is selected for change.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — 9.1 Linux Storage Architecture

6. 9.2 Block Devices

A block device exposes addressable storage blocks. Linux paths can include /dev/sda, /dev/vda, or /dev/nvme0n1, depending on the device and driver. Partition names follow device-specific conventions, such as /dev/nvme0n1p1.

These short names can change when hardware discovery order changes. Persistent paths under /dev/disk/by-id and filesystem UUIDs provide more stable references for appropriate tasks.

Before any destructive operation, match the guest device to the hypervisor or hardware inventory using size, serial, model, and relationships. Confirm that it is not a parent of the root filesystem, swap, an encrypted mapping, LVM, RAID, or another active consumer. No single “not mounted” check proves a device is unused.

Linux example — 9.2

List physical and virtual block-device identities.

What to check: Cross-check serials and sizes with the console; a device letter alone is not a durable identity.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — 9.2 Block Devices

8. 9.3 lsblk

lsblk displays block devices and relationships. Request explicit columns because default output can change between versions and may omit the evidence you need.

The tree helps show partitions and device-mapper layers. A blank filesystem column does not prove a device contains nothing valuable; signatures may be absent, unsupported, hidden behind another layer, or damaged.

For scripts, use documented structured output such as --json with explicit columns rather than parsing aligned terminal text. Even structured discovery should not automatically authorize erasure. Human approval or an equally strong provisioning contract must establish that the device is intentionally disposable. (R20)

Linux example — 9.3

Select lsblk columns explicitly.

What to check: Explicit columns avoid depending on changing default output.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — 9.3 lsblk

11. 9.4 blkid

blkid probes block-device metadata and can report filesystem type, UUID, and label. It complements lsblk by identifying recognized on-disk signatures.

A filesystem UUID identifies the filesystem, not necessarily the underlying physical disk. Reformatting creates a new filesystem identity; cloning can copy an existing UUID and create ambiguity when both copies are attached.

Use direct, appropriately privileged probing when you need current metadata rather than relying on possibly incomplete cached information. After cloning or storage replacement, verify that persistent mount references identify exactly the intended filesystem. A boot failure after a disk change can be an identity problem rather than missing data.

Linux example — 9.4

Read filesystem signatures.

What to check: A UUID identifies a filesystem signature; cloned filesystems may duplicate it.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — 9.4 blkid

14. 9.5 Partition Tables

A partition table describes regions of a disk assigned to partitions. It is separate from the filesystems inside those regions. Changing a partition boundary does not automatically transform or resize the filesystem it contains.

Preserve the starting sector of an existing filesystem when performing an approved growth operation. Moving the start is a different and much riskier task. Before changes, save the partition layout and ensure the backup is stored somewhere other than the device being modified.

For a new lab disk, plan alignment, boot requirements, data separation, and future growth. For an existing production disk, do not replace the table simply because a tool presents a cleaner-looking layout. The table is a map to existing data, not a cosmetic preference.

Linux example — 9.5

List partition layouts without writing them.

What to check: No partition table is changed by this listing operation.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — 9.5 Partition Tables

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — 9.5 Partition Tables

16. 9.6 GPT and MBR

GPT is the modern partition-table format commonly paired with UEFI systems and supports more flexible partitioning than the older MBR scheme. MBR has historical size and partition-count limitations whose practical effect depends on sector size and layout.

GPT includes redundant metadata, but that does not make it a data backup. Corrupting a filesystem or losing the device is still a separate failure. Likewise, a valid partition table does not prove every partition contains a valid filesystem.

Use the format appropriate to the platform and operating-system requirements. Converting a live boot disk between schemes is a planned migration, not a routine command to try during an unrelated outage.

Linux example — 9.6

Inspect partition-table types.

What to check: GPT and DOS/MBR are partition formats, distinct from ext4 or XFS filesystems.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — 9.6 GPT and MBR

18. 9.7 fdisk and parted

fdisk and parted inspect and modify partition tables. Their write operations can destroy access to data. Learn them first on a disk-image file or a clearly identified disposable virtual disk.

Change — new user-owned image file only.

The ext4 token is a partition hint; this command does not create an ext4 filesystem inside the partition. The image exercise teaches table structure without selecting a real block device. Remove the known image and empty directory when finished. Do not replace the image path with a system disk to “make the example real.”

Linux example — 9.7

Use fdisk in listing mode and inspect parted help.

What to check: Interactive write commands must be restricted to a positively identified disposable disk.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — 9.7 fdisk and parted

21. 9.8 Creating Filesystems

A filesystem organizes storage into objects, metadata, and allocation structures. mkfs.ext4 and mkfs.xfs create different filesystem formats. They do not preserve the previous contents as a recoverable version.

Before formatting, establish the target identity, required filesystem, label or UUID plan, mount location, capacity, backup status, and approval. Existing signatures are a reason to stop and investigate, not a reason to add a force option automatically.

The worked example formats a newly created ordinary file, then mounts it through a loop device. This is sufficient to learn filesystem creation and mounting. Production devices add additional requirements around alignment, encryption, storage redundancy, support, and recovery.

Linux example — 9.8

Create a filesystem inside a newly created file, not a disk.

What to check: -F is used only on this fresh regular-file image; never substitute an existing device.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — 9.8 Creating Filesystems

23. 9.9 ext4

ext4 is a widely used Linux filesystem supporting journaling and established administration tools. Journaling improves recovery of filesystem consistency after some interruptions; it does not guarantee that every application write was durably committed.

resize2fs manages ext-family filesystem size under supported conditions. Growth can often occur while mounted; shrinking requires an offline procedure and careful coordination with the underlying device. The exact support depends on the filesystem and kernel environment.

Use e2fsck for appropriate offline checks, not a generic repair command against a busy mounted filesystem. Before any repair, preserve data or an image when possible and investigate underlying storage errors. Repeated repair without fixing failing hardware can worsen data loss. (R21)

Linux example — 9.9

Inspect the ext4 image created in section 9.8.

What to check: Requires e2fsprogs; inspect block counts, UUID, and filesystem features.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — 9.9 ext4

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — 9.9 ext4

25. 9.10 XFS

XFS is another mature Linux filesystem used commonly in enterprise environments. It supports online growth and has its own tools, including xfs_growfs, xfs_info, and xfs_repair.

For the RHEL 9 teaching baseline, plan XFS capacity changes as grow-only. Do not shrink the underlying logical volume beneath an XFS filesystem. To move to a smaller allocation, create a new appropriately sized filesystem and perform a verified migration or restore.

xfs_growfs normally operates on the mounted filesystem’s mount point. xfs_repair has different requirements and risks from ext4’s repair tools. A familiar-looking filesystem problem does not justify using another filesystem’s repair command. (R22)

Linux example — 9.10

Inspect XFS capabilities without formatting storage.

What to check: An empty mount listing can simply mean this host has no mounted XFS filesystem.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — 9.10 XFS

27. 9.11 Mounting Filesystems

Mounting attaches a filesystem to a directory in the visible tree. The directory must exist, and existing contents beneath it become hidden while the mount is active. A mount can have options governing execution, devices, privilege bits, access mode, and other behavior.

Use findmnt for precise inspection rather than parsing an unbounded human-oriented mount listing in automation. Mount options such as nosuid, nodev, and noexec can reduce certain risks, but they are not a complete sandbox.

Unmounting requires that the filesystem no longer be in use under normal conditions. Diagnose users with tools such as fuser or lsof; do not immediately reach for forced or lazy unmounting on a service’s active data path. (R23)

Linux example — 9.11

Mount the section 9.8 image read-only in the lab VM.

What to check: Confirm ro in mount options; unmount before leaving the exercise.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — 9.11 Mounting Filesystems

30. 9.12 /etc/fstab

/etc/fstab describes persistent mounts and swap according to fields for source, target, type, options, dump, and filesystem-check order. On systemd systems, a generator translates relevant entries into units.

A typical data entry might use a filesystem UUID and an explicit mount point. The actual UUID must come from the intended device. Do not copy an example UUID from documentation.

Before applying changes, save a protected copy and use findmnt --verify --verbose to check the table. Run systemctl daemon-reload after changing fstab on a systemd host, then test the specific mount. A successful mount test is stronger than syntax alone. Do not reboot to discover a typo that could have been checked while access still worked.

Linux example — 9.12

Validate fstab without mounting every entry.

What to check: Validation can reveal syntax and target issues; successful checks do not prove boot-time availability.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — 9.12 /etc/fstab

32. 9.13 UUIDs

A UUID is an identifier used by many filesystem and storage components. Filesystem UUIDs are useful in fstab because short device names may change. Partition UUIDs identify partitions and are not the same thing as filesystem UUIDs.

A cloned disk can contain duplicated identifiers. Attaching both original and clone may make an otherwise reasonable persistent reference ambiguous. Change identifiers only through the correct tool and with an understanding of every reference that depends on them.

After reformatting, update the mount configuration to the new filesystem identity. The mount point name does not somehow remember which newly created filesystem belongs there.

Linux example — 9.13

Compare filesystem UUIDs with persistent configuration.

What to check: Match the intended filesystem, not merely a familiar disk name.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — 9.13 UUIDs

35. 9.14 Swap

Swap provides backing storage for selected memory pages. It can be a partition, logical volume, or supported file. It may help absorb temporary pressure, but it is not equivalent to RAM in latency or throughput.

Inspect before changing. Enabling or disabling swap affects memory pressure and can fail or disrupt workloads if insufficient RAM is available. Do not run swapoff -a on a busy machine merely to make a display look cleaner.

Swap-file requirements differ across filesystems, especially around holes, copy-on-write behavior, and allocation. Follow the filesystem’s supported procedure. Protect swap containing sensitive memory through the organization’s encryption policy, including hibernation and boot requirements where relevant.

Linux example — 9.14

Inspect active swap.

What to check: No listed swap may be intentional; decide using workload and memory policy.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — 9.14 Swap

38. 9.15 Disk Usage

Storage usage can mean allocated blocks, apparent file size, filesystem capacity, snapshots, thin-pool consumption, or underlying provisioned storage. These measurements are related but not identical.

A sparse file can have a large apparent size while using few blocks. A snapshot can retain old blocks no longer visible in the current filesystem view. A deleted-but-open file can consume space without appearing in an ordinary directory scan.

Ask which layer’s capacity is exhausted. A filesystem may have free space while its thin pool is nearly full, or the underlying cloud disk may be large while the filesystem remains small. Monitoring must cover the layers that can independently stop writes.

Linux example — 9.15

Measure your own home directory.

What to check: du measures visible file allocation; df reports capacity for the containing filesystem.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — 9.15 Disk Usage

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — 9.15 Disk Usage

40. 9.16 df and du

df reports capacity and usage from filesystem accounting. du walks reachable files and totals their usage according to its options. They answer different questions and need not agree exactly.

-x keeps the du walk on one filesystem, and -d1 limits displayed depth in GNU du. Even a bounded-depth report can scan many descendants, so consider load on a busy host.

Differences can result from open deleted files, inaccessible paths, reserved blocks, metadata, sparse allocation, snapshots, or mounts hiding underlying files. Do not “correct” the discrepancy by deleting random large directories. Use it as a clue about which objects each tool can see.

Linux example — 9.16

Compare bytes and inodes for a path.

What to check: Permission errors can make du incomplete; bytes and inodes are separate exhaustion modes.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — 9.16 df and du

43. 9.17 Filesystem Repair

Repair modifies filesystem metadata to recover a usable structure. It can discard damaged information and should not be treated as a harmless diagnostic. Prefer read-only assessment and a recoverable image or backup before destructive repair when feasible.

Use the filesystem-specific tool and its required mount state. ext4 checks normally use e2fsck on an unmounted filesystem. XFS repair uses xfs_repair on an unmounted filesystem; forcing log destruction is a high-risk last resort with possible data loss, not a default flag.

If storage hardware is failing, repeated scans may increase stress. Escalate to an appropriate recovery procedure and preserve the best available copy. A repaired filesystem also needs application-level validation: directory consistency does not prove a database is logically correct.

Linux example — 9.17

Perform a nonwriting ext4 check on the unmounted image from 9.8.

What to check: Run only while the image is unmounted; -n refuses repairs and -f forces a check.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — 9.17 Filesystem Repair

45. 9.18 Expanding Storage

Expand from the outside inward: provision more device capacity, extend a partition if used, extend a physical volume if used, allocate logical-volume space if used, and finally grow the filesystem. The exact sequence depends on the actual stack.

After each step, inspect the layer’s reported size before continuing. A command that enlarges a logical volume without growing its filesystem has not yet supplied the application with more file capacity.

Growth still needs a backup and a rollback or recovery plan. “Usually online” is not the same as “risk-free.” Verify application writes, free capacity, persistent mount identity, and behavior after a controlled reboot when the maintenance plan permits it.

Linux example — 9.18

Inspect storage layers before planning expansion.

What to check: Device, partition, volume, and filesystem growth may require separate operations.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — 9.18 Expanding Storage

47. Requirement and safety boundary

Create an ext4 filesystem, mount it, store a small file, and unmount it without touching a real disk. Use a disposable VM with e2fsprogs, util-linux tools, and loop-mount support. The image must be a newly created file in the unique lab directory.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — Requirement and safety boundary

48. Command walkthrough

Destructive lab — formatting is confined to a new image file.

The force flag is used only because the target is the newly created ordinary image file. It must not become a habit applied to a device with existing signatures. Stop if the path does not exactly match the new lab image.

The apparent 256 MiB image size and its actual allocated blocks can differ because the file began sparse. The nested filesystem has metadata overhead, so usable capacity is smaller than its nominal container size.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — Command walkthrough

51. Recovery and cleanup

Leave the mount directory before unmounting. If unmount reports busy, identify the open working directory or process rather than forcing it.

The final query should no longer find an exact mount at that path and may return a nonzero status for that reason. Only after verifying unmount should you remove the known image and directories:

This is a lab reset, not a backup strategy. The entire nested filesystem disappears when its image is removed.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — Recovery and cleanup

54. Practice and implementation lab

Draw the storage stack for the filesystem containing your home directory. Identify every visible block layer and distinguish what is known inside the guest from what belongs to the hypervisor.

Create a partitioned image with parted, inspect it, and explain why a partition type hint does not create a usable filesystem. Then inspect a real fstab entry without changing it and identify its source, mount point, filesystem, and options.

Check your understanding. Why can enlarging a cloud disk leave df unchanged? Inner layers may not have grown. Does a blank FSTYPE authorize formatting? No. Can the RHEL 9 XFS lab filesystem be made smaller by reducing its LV? No; that would cut storage from beneath the filesystem and risk data loss.

Chapter takeaway. Identify the storage stack and its ownership before changing it, and verify every layer independently.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch011.xhtml — Practice and implementation lab

55. Detect inode exhaustion independently of bytes

Use a controlled capacity fixture rather than filling the real filesystem. The solution checks the stated outcome explicitly. These fixture results do not establish that a real privileged service is configured correctly.

SOURCE: Detect inode exhaustion independently of bytes
